chapters.title: The weariness of life under the sun

parts.text: The Preacher, identified as David’s son and king in Jerusalem, begins, ‘Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.’ He asks what lasting profit people gain from their labour. Generations pass while the earth remains, and sun, wind, and rivers continue familiar cycles. Human desire is never fully satisfied. What appears new has precedents, and both earlier and later generations fade from remembrance.

The Preacher recounts applying wisdom to everything done under heaven. He finds the task grievous and the works done under the sun to be vanity and vexation of spirit: crooked things remain crooked, and missing things cannot simply be supplied. His pursuit includes wisdom, madness, and folly, but increased knowledge also increases awareness of sorrow rather than removing it.

chapters.title: Pleasure and achievement cannot defeat mortality

parts.text: The Preacher tests pleasure, laughter, wine, building projects, gardens, servants, livestock, treasure, and music. He becomes exceedingly great and denies himself no desired enjoyment, while retaining his wisdom. Yet when he surveys his achievements, he finds no lasting profit under the sun. The pleasure accompanying the work does not make its results permanent.

Wisdom is better than folly, but both wise and foolish people die and are forgotten. The worker must leave his possessions to someone who may misuse them, turning accomplishment into frustration. Nevertheless, eating, drinking, and enjoying labour are received as gifts from God’s hand, who gives wisdom and joy rather than allowing human effort to control every outcome.

The Preacher lists contrasting seasons: birth and death, planting and uprooting, weeping and laughter, silence and speech, war and peace. God makes everything fitting in its time, yet people cannot comprehend his work from beginning to end. Joy, doing good, and enjoyment of labour are gifts. God’s enduring work calls for reverence rather than human attempts to add to or subtract from it.

Wickedness appears even where judgment should be found, but God will judge both righteous and wicked. Human beings and animals alike die and return to dust. The Preacher questions what people can know of what follows and commends enjoyment of one’s present work, since no one can bring him to see what shall be after him.

chapters.title: Oppression, rivalry, and the value of companionship

parts.text: The Preacher observes the tears of the oppressed, who have no comforter against powerful oppressors. He considers their suffering so grievous that the dead, or even those never born, seem better placed. Work driven by envy is also empty, while idleness destroys and restless accumulation leaves the solitary worker unable to explain whom he is serving.

Two people benefit from shared work, mutual help when one falls, warmth, and resistance against attack. A threefold cord is not easily broken. The chapter then contrasts a poor, wise youth with an old king who refuses advice. Even a popular successor cannot rely on lasting public approval, showing the instability of political success.

chapters.title: Reverent speech and the limits of wealth

parts.text: Those entering God’s house should listen carefully rather than offer the sacrifice of fools. God is in heaven and people are on earth, so rash speech and excessive words are unfitting. Vows should be fulfilled promptly; it is better not to vow than to promise and fail. Reverence must govern worship and speech.

The Preacher notes oppression within human administration and then considers wealth’s disappointments. Money does not satisfy the lover of money, possessions attract consumers, and anxious riches can rob their owner of sleep. Wealth may disappear, and death carries nothing away. Enjoying one’s allotted work and possessions is therefore a gift from God, not a secure result of accumulation alone.

The Preacher describes a grievous situation: someone receives wealth and honour but lacks the ability to enjoy them, while a stranger benefits. A long life and many children do not resolve a life without satisfaction or even an honourable burial. In such circumstances, he says an untimely birth has more rest than a person who never experiences good.

Labour feeds the mouth but does not end desire. Enjoying what is actually present is preferable to restless longing for what is not. Human beings cannot contend successfully with the One mightier than themselves, determine fully what is good throughout their brief life, or explain what will happen after them.

chapters.title: Wisdom learns from sorrow and acknowledges its limits

parts.text: A good name, sober reflection at a funeral, wise rebuke, and patient endurance are valued above perfume, feasting, empty laughter, and pride. Hasty anger and romanticizing former times are questioned. Wisdom provides protection and preserves life, but it cannot undo God’s work. Prosperity and adversity alike should lead people to recognize that their future is not fully within their grasp.

The Preacher observes outcomes that seem contrary to merit and warns against self-destructive excess, calling instead for fear of God. No one is wholly without sin, so overheard insults should be weighed with self-knowledge. His search for wisdom exposes both seductive snares and his own limits. He concludes that God made humanity upright, but people pursued many inventions.

chapters.title: Authority, delayed judgment, and unexplained outcomes

parts.text: Wisdom affects a person’s bearing and helps discern appropriate action under royal authority. The Preacher counsels respect for the king’s command, especially in view of the oath of God. Yet neither rulers nor subjects can control the future, retain their spirit indefinitely, or escape death. Human government can become a means by which one person harms another.

Delayed punishment encourages evil, and events sometimes appear to reward the wicked while burdening the righteous. Nevertheless, the Preacher affirms that it will be well with those who fear God. He commends receiving ordinary enjoyment within one’s allotted labour, while acknowledging that even diligent wisdom cannot fully discover all God’s work under the sun.

The Preacher reflects that righteous and wicked people share the certainty of death, while present circumstances do not disclose everything about God’s regard. The living still have opportunity, whereas the dead no longer participate in the activities under the sun. He therefore commends joyful meals, clean garments, loving marriage, and wholehearted work during the life God gives.

Success is not guaranteed by speed, strength, wisdom, or skill, because unexpected events overtake everyone. A poor wise man once saved a small city from a powerful king, yet was forgotten. Wisdom is better than strength or weapons, but society may neglect it, and one sinner can undo much good.

chapters.title: Small follies and the need for practical wisdom

parts.text: A little folly can spoil a reputation as dead flies spoil ointment. Wisdom and foolishness direct people differently, and a calm response may avert trouble with an angry ruler. The Preacher notes the disorder created when folly receives high position. Ordinary work also carries hazards, making preparation and skill, like sharpening a blunt tool, preferable to wasted effort.

Wise speech is gracious, but foolish talk grows into destructive nonsense. A land suffers under immature, indulgent rulers and benefits when leaders exercise disciplined strength. Neglect allows a house to decay. The chapter ends with caution about careless criticism of rulers and the wealthy, since even words spoken privately can travel unexpectedly.

chapters.title: Act faithfully amid uncertainty and remember judgment

parts.text: The Preacher urges generous, distributed action rather than paralysis before uncertain events. Rain falls, trees fall, and excessive attention to winds and clouds prevents sowing and reaping. Just as people cannot fully explain life forming in the womb, they cannot comprehend all God’s work. They should therefore sow morning and evening without knowing which effort will prosper.

Life and daylight are pleasant, and years may rightly be enjoyed, but coming darkness must also be remembered. The young are invited to rejoice and pursue life’s opportunities while recognizing that God will bring their conduct into judgment. Sorrow and evil should be put away, because youth itself passes quickly.

chapters.title: Remember your Creator before the days fade

parts.text: The young are urged to remember their Creator before declining years arrive. Poetic images of darkened lights, trembling guardians, failing grinders, shut doors, and fading desire portray approaching frailty and death. Before life’s cord and vessel are broken, remembrance is needed. Dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God who gave it; the Preacher again declares the vanity of earthly life.

The closing description honours the Preacher’s careful teaching and truthful words, comparing wise instruction to goads and securely fixed nails. Endless books and study can weary the body. The final duty is to fear God and keep his commandments, because every deed, including hidden good and evil, will come into judgment.
